title: Globalisation & multinationals
examples: What are the main reasons why a company might decide to sell products in many different countries?
Can you explain the positive and negative effects of big companies operating in many countries?
How does globalisation help small businesses expand their reach?

explain.say: Today we are looking at why businesses expand globally. Sometimes companies want to sell their products in many different countries. This process is called globalisation. We will explore the reasons behind this big move.

items: Lower production costs in other nations

explain.say: Another key reason is accessing different raw materials. A company might need a specific metal only found in one country. This forces them to set up there. Think about the need for unique resources.
Sometimes, local markets are too competitive at home. A business might move abroad to find a less crowded market. This helps them grow without facing too much local rivalry.
Now let us look at the impacts. One positive impact is job creation in the host country. Multinational companies build factories and employ many local people. This boosts the local economy.
A negative impact is sometimes the loss of local control. Big foreign companies might push out small local businesses. This can change the character of the local economy.
In everyday life, think about your favorite brand of clothing. If they sell everywhere, it is globalisation. They use global supply chains to get materials and sell the final product worldwide.

faq.q: What exactly is a multinational corporation?
faq.a: It is a large company that operates in several countries. These companies manage their business activities in more than one nation. You might also hear it called a global firm.
asks: How many countries must a company be in to be multinational?

faq.q: Does globalisation only help rich countries?
faq.a: No, it can affect developing nations too. While it brings investment, it can also exploit cheap labour. Some argue it creates an unfair economic gap.
asks: Does it only benefit the West?
What are the downsides for poorer nations?

faq.a: This means a company invests money directly into a foreign country. They might build a new factory or buy a local business. It is more than just sending money.
asks: What is the difference between trade and investment?
Does FDI mean the company owns things there?
Is investing abroad the same as exporting?

faq.q: Why do businesses want to lower their costs by going global?
faq.a: Labour costs are often much lower in developing economies. By moving production there, companies can make their goods cheaper to sell. This is a major economic driver.
asks: Why are wages different in different countries?
Is cheap labour always the best option?
How much can a company save by moving production?

faq.q: What is a local business struggling with when globalisation happens?
faq.a: They might struggle because global chains offer lower prices due to massive scale. They cannot compete on cost or product range alone. They need a unique selling point.
asks: How do small shops survive large stores?
What is the biggest threat to local markets?
Can small businesses compete with global brands?

facts: Multinational corporations operate in multiple countries. This is a key aspect of globalisation. They manage activities across borders.
One reason for global expansion is accessing cheaper labour costs. This reduces the overall cost of production for the company.
A positive impact is the transfer of technology to local workers. This improves the skills and infrastructure of the host country.
A negative impact can be the decline of local industries. Small, established businesses may struggle against large international competitors.

quiz.say: A company moves its car assembly plant from its home country to a country with lower wages. This is mainly due to:
quiz.why: This directly addresses the economic reason for moving production overseas.

wrong.0: Tariffs are taxes on goods, not the main reason for shifting the entire factory.
wrong.1: High competition usually pushes companies to find new markets, not just move production.
wrong.3: While materials matter, the primary driver for moving assembly is usually cost.

quiz.say: If a company sells its unique brand of coffee beans in every continent, it is demonstrating:
quiz.why: Selling across continents shows they are tapping into a worldwide customer base.

wrong.0: Saturation means the market is full; selling everywhere means they are expanding beyond limits.
wrong.2: This describes owning all stages of production, not just selling widely.
wrong.3: This refers to having many sources of materials, not selling in many places.

quiz.say: Which outcome represents a negative impact on the host country?
quiz.why: This shows a direct negative consequence for the existing local economy.

wrong.0: Technology transfer is generally considered a positive economic benefit.
wrong.1: This is a benefit to the company, not necessarily a negative impact on the country.
wrong.3: This is a positive outcome, not a negative one.
